name: DriveSafe
summary: DriveSafe watches for prolonged eye closure, yawning and distraction in webcam video. Our team tested the detector in day and night conditions and used an Arduino simulation to explore how a vehicle could respond to persistent warnings.
question: When does an ordinary blink become a reason to warn a driver?
context: A driver’s eyes and mouth move even when they are alert. We needed to distinguish brief movements from persistent signs of fatigue, keep the landmarks visible in low light and decide how the warning should change if a driver recovered or continued to look away.
role: On a three-person team, I connected the webcam to OpenCV and dlib, worked on low-light frame normalization and implemented the timing logic for escalating alerts. In Tinkercad, I integrated the ultrasonic sensors and motors and designed the staged deceleration and stopping logic.

work.title: Track the face across lighting conditions
work.text: OpenCV prepared the live frames and dlib located 68 facial landmarks. Measurements around the eyes and mouth captured prolonged closure, dozing and yawning. Low-light normalization helped keep landmarks visible in nighttime video.

work.title: Give the warning a memory
work.text: Timing the eye and mouth measurements let the software treat a blink differently from sustained closure. Persistent signs triggered stronger visual and audible warnings. The test cases also covered recovery when the driver became alert again.

work.title: Test the motor response in simulation
work.text: We modeled four ultrasonic sensors and a motor circuit on an Arduino in Tinkercad. In the simulation, sustained warnings triggered staged deceleration, and an obstacle could trigger a stop. We checked the response through the simulated motor speed and serial output.

outcome: The team measured 98.2% detection accuracy in daytime testing and 98% at night. The capstone received an A (10/10). The submitted report documents the detector results and the simulated motor responses separately.
limits: The detection figures come from the team’s test conditions. The motor and obstacle responses were tested in Tinkercad. Road testing would be needed to evaluate vehicle behavior.
takeaway: Detection and response needed separate tests. A correct landmark reading was only the first step. We also checked what happened to the warning and motor state as the driver recovered or an obstacle appeared.
subtitle: Read signs of drowsiness and time the warning.
plainRole: Worked on landmark tracking, low-light frames, timed alerts and Arduino motor logic.
plainResult: Team testing recorded 98.2% daytime and 98% nighttime detection accuracy. The capstone earned an A (10/10).
plainLimit: The motor and obstacle response was evaluated in Tinkercad.

name: Shabad Shazam
summary: Hear a Gurbani recording and want to find it again? Shabad Shazam uses a short microphone clip to look up the hymn, performer and listening links in a catalog of recordings.
question: How do you find a hymn when all you have is a few seconds of audio?
context: A listener can recognize a shabad, a sacred Sikh hymn, without knowing the title or who is singing it. The app starts with what the listener has in hand. A brief recording from a phone microphone is enough to start a search.
role: I’m building the Flutter and Dart app, its Python recognition service and the ingestion tools that populate the reference catalog. I set up Docker Compose so the FastAPI service and PostgreSQL database run together locally.

work.title: Give each recording a fingerprint
work.text: During catalog ingestion, the service finds peaks in a recording’s frequency spectrum. It pairs nearby peaks and stores a hash of each pair with the recording ID and its position in the track.

work.title: Find where a clip belongs
work.text: A microphone clip can start halfway through a performance. The service looks up its peak-pair hashes in PostgreSQL. When multiple matches point to the same recording at a consistent time offset, they provide evidence for a match.

work.title: Return a result a listener can use
work.text: The Flutter app sends the clip to FastAPI and displays the matching hymn, performer and listening links. A CSV-driven import keeps that metadata paired with each indexed recording, and local history lets listeners revisit earlier results.

outcome: A listener can go from a short recording to a named performance, open a listening link and find the result again in the app’s history.
limits: The search covers recordings already indexed in PostgreSQL. A different performance of the same hymn needs its own reference fingerprints.
takeaway: Two performers can sing the same hymn and produce different fingerprints. Keeping the hymn title and the recording identity separate lets the app explain exactly what it matched.
subtitle: Identify a Gurbani recording from a few seconds of audio.
plainRole: Building the mobile app, fingerprint matcher and recording catalog.
plainResult: One clip returns a matching catalog recording with hymn, performer and listening links.
plainLimit: Each performance needs a reference recording in the catalog.

name: Neuro Data Lab
summary: Could a game tell which way someone was watching it move? Our four-person team built an EEG toolbox and compared five classifiers on brain signals recorded during forward and backward movement cues.
question: Can a classifier tell forward from backward movement using EEG recordings?
context: Before an EEG signal could become a game command, we needed a way to capture and label examples of both directions. Participants wore a 14-channel EMOTIV EPOC X headset while a first-person simulation showed forward and backward movement. The timing of each cue gave us a label for the corresponding signal.
role: I led the four-person team, coordinated access to the headset and organized participant recording sessions. I built Python and PyQt features to import recordings, prepare signals with FastICA and display the results of five scikit-learn classifiers.

work.title: Record a signal with a known label
work.text: We timed the movement cues, checked headset contact in EmotivPro and exported the 14-channel recordings to CSV. Pairing signal segments with the direction on screen gave us a two-class dataset for offline evaluation.

work.title: Turn recordings into model inputs
work.text: The PyQt toolbox brought file import, signal preparation and model results into one interface. FastICA separated components of the mixed EEG signals before we compared the classifiers.

work.title: Compare what the models get right
work.text: We evaluated Extra Trees, random forest, k-nearest neighbors, a decision tree and a support vector machine. Extra Trees led on accuracy, recall and F1. K-nearest neighbors had the highest precision at 95.24%.

outcome: Extra Trees reached 95.45% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.956 on the project’s offline evaluation. The jury awarded the capstone an A, worth 10/10 grade points.
limits: We evaluated labeled recordings of people watching movement cues. A live game controller would also need tests with new participants and sessions, plus a way to turn predictions into timely commands.
takeaway: The cue schedule mattered as much as the classifier. A model score becomes interpretable only when every EEG segment can be traced to the movement a participant saw.
subtitle: Classify movement cues from 14-channel EEG recordings.
plainRole: Led four people, coordinated recording sessions and built the PyQt analysis features.
plainResult: Extra Trees led five classifiers with 95.45% offline accuracy. The jury awarded an A (10/10).
plainLimit: The evaluation used recorded cues. Live game control remained a next step.

name: MED-e-CARE
summary: MED-e-CARE connects pharmacy orders to stock on hand. Customers can order available medicines, administrators update inventory, and NGOs can find medicines eligible for free distribution by expiry date.
question: How can one inventory serve a pharmacy customer and an NGO?
context: During the pandemic, our five-person team designed a pharmacy application for people ordering from home. An NGO needed a different view of the same stock. It had to see which medicines were available for free distribution while they still had usable shelf life.
role: I connected the HTML ordering interface to the Python backend and SQL database. I implemented the stock check at order placement and helped model login, ordering and the relationships among users, inventory and orders.

work.title: Make availability part of checkout
work.text: When a customer selected a medicine, the backend checked the inventory record before allowing the order to proceed. An out-of-stock selection returned an error so the customer could revise the order.

work.title: Give administrators a working record
work.text: Administrators could update quantities, expiry dates and other stock details, then track orders and sales. Customers could revisit order history through their accounts. Our UML use cases traced those interactions to the underlying records.

work.title: Use shelf life to build the NGO list
work.text: The project specified a free-order list for medicines with six to twelve months left before expiry. An NGO could browse eligible stock and request a quantity through its own ordering flow.

outcome: The project delivered an academic web application that linked customer orders to inventory, handled unavailable stock explicitly and gave NGOs a separate view of eligible medicines.
limits: We assessed the application through its academic workflows for ordering, stock management and NGO availability. The submitted report describes the system design and use cases.
takeaway: Availability meant two different things in this application. A customer needed a stock count, while an NGO also needed to know whether a batch fell inside the expiry window. Both rules belonged in the data model.
subtitle: Connect pharmacy orders to stock and shelf life.
plainRole: Connected checkout to Python and SQL, implemented stock checks and helped design the relational model.
plainResult: Customers could place in-stock orders, while NGOs could find eligible medicines through a dedicated flow.
plainLimit: Academic web application developed during the COVID-19 pandemic.
